earlier_parts.problem:
The function $p(x)$ is defined as

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ g(x), & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find the value of the constant $k$ that makes $p(x)$ continuous at $x=3.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $k\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}

feedback.worked_solution:
We have the piecewise function

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ 8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}, & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

At $x=3,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & =p(3) \\  & =k+10,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}) \\  & =8(3)-\frac{2}{3}(3)^{3} \\  & =24-18 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $p(x)$ to be continuous at $x=3,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) \\ k+10 & =6 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p(x)$ is continuous at $x=3$ when $k=-4.$

We know that 

$$
\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Applying this formula and the constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-4\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}) \\  & =8-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =8-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the second derivative, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

earlier_parts.problem:
The equation of the normal to the curve $y=f(x)\cdot h(x)$ at the point where $x=\pi $ is

                            
                                    
                                        
                                        $\,y=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        .

feedback.worked_solution:
When $x=\pi ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =f(\pi )\cdot h(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{\pi }\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{\pi }\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 4, we found that the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)\cdot h(x)$ at the point where $x=\pi $ is $m=2{e}^{\pi }.$ Therefore, the slope of the normal ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{2{e}^{\pi }}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{\pi }}(x-\pi ) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2{e}^{\pi }}+\frac{\pi }{2{e}^{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

We apply the quotient rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f}{h}) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot h(x)-f(x)\cdot {h}^{′}(x)}{[h(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})}^{′}\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}}{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{16{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{16{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$
